summary: Specifies how Standard apt-X and Enhanced apt-X audio is packetized into RTP packets, supporting several related channels in one payload and SDP signalling.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to cut up sound from a certain audio format into small pieces to send over the internet.

questions: how is apt-x sent over rtp
what is the audio/aptx media type
what is the default rtp packet interval for apt-x
subtitle: How to carry apt-X and Enhanced apt-X compressed audio, including multichannel audio, in RTP packets.

tldr.problem: Standard apt-X and Enhanced apt-X are proprietary audio codecs with no standard way to send their output in RTP packets or describe it in SDP.
tldr.mechanism: The coded samples are packed byte by byte in big-endian order, channels are interleaved per sampling instant, the default packet interval is 4 milliseconds, and a new media type audio/aptx carries the settings into SDP.
tldr.outcome: Any RTP sender and receiver can exchange apt-X audio, with embedded autosync, auxiliary data and stereo pairing signaled out of band.

today: RFC 7310 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
RFC 7310 specifies how audio coded with Standard apt-X or Enhanced apt-X is packetized into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550). It also defines how to describe such a stream with the Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566).

The payload format can carry several related audio channels in a single RTP payload. The document registers one media type for it, audio/aptx.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper explains how to put a certain kind of squeezed sound into the envelopes the internet uses for live audio, and how to write on the envelope what is inside.

sections.title: The apt-X Codecs
sections.content:
Both codecs are proprietary and based on Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation principles. The RFC states that their internals are not described in standards or reference documents, but their data interfaces are simple enough that packetization does not need to know the coded stream syntax.

The coded bit rate is constant and equal to 1/4 of the uncoded bit rate. For example, a 1.536-Mbit/s stereo stream (two 16-bit channels at 48 kHz) is coded at 384 kbit/s. Four successive PCM samples per channel become one coded sample: 16 bits for Standard apt-X, and 16 or 24 bits for Enhanced apt-X.

Coded streams can optionally carry autosync information and an auxiliary data channel inside the coded audio at no extra overhead. The auxiliary channel runs at 1/4 of the sample frequency, so 12 kbit/s for one channel at 48 kHz. Two channels can be stereo-paired to share these features, which is off by default. A decoder not told about these settings plays out uncoded PCM samples with a loss of quality, which can be significant for Standard apt-X.

Because these features change nothing in the packet layout, they must be announced out of band, for example in SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The squeezer turns every four sound snapshots into one small snapshot, so the stream is a quarter of the size. If the listener does not know the secret settings, the music comes out crackly.

sections.title: Packing Samples into RTP
sections.content:
The encoder MUST be given a number S of input samples that is a multiple of 4 and produces exactly S/4 coded samples. Because each coded sample is 16 or 24 bits, the output is a whole number of bytes, and packetization is done byte by byte.

The RTP header has no special requirements. A dynamic payload type MUST be used, and the timestamp reflects the instant the first (oldest) audio sample in the packet was sampled. Coded samples are packed contiguously in network byte order (big-endian), most significant bit first, oldest sample first. A packet MUST hold a whole number of coded samples.

For multichannel audio in one RTP stream, the coded samples of one sampling instant are interleaved into a block using the standard channel ordering of RFC 3551. All coded samples of one instant MUST be in the same packet, and all channels in the stream MUST use the same sampling frequency.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a row of kids each saying one word, always in the same order, oldest word first. Everyone for one moment goes into the same bus, and the bus keeps the order every time.

sections.title: Packetization Interval and Example
sections.content:
The default packetization interval MUST be 4 milliseconds, and all implementations MUST support it. If a whole number of coded samples per channel does not fit in 4 ms, the interval is rounded down. At 11025, 22050 or 44100 Hz the interval becomes 3.99 milliseconds.

The RFC explains the trade-off: shorter packets cut delay but cost bandwidth, while longer packets have less header overhead but add delay and make loss more noticeable. Four milliseconds is chosen as a balance suitable for interactive use.

The worked example is a six-channel 24-bit signal sampled at 48 kHz. Uncoded, it is 6 * 24 * 48000 = 6.912 Mbit/s. Enhanced apt-X with 24-bit coded samples brings that to 1.728 Mbit/s, and each 4 ms packet carries 864 bytes holding 48 coded samples per channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Short packets are like sending many small parcels: quick, but lots of wrapping. Long parcels waste less wrapping but take longer to fill. The RFC picks small ones, 4 milliseconds each.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Signaling
sections.content:
The media type is audio/aptx. Required parameters are rate (the RTP clock rate, equal to the sampling rate in Hz), channels, variant (standard or enhanced) and bitresolution (16 for Standard; 16 or 24 for Enhanced).

Optional parameters are ptime (default 4 ms), maxptime, stereo-channel-pairs, embedded-autosync-channels and embedded-aux-channels. A channel MUST NOT be paired with more than one other channel. For a pair, the first channel MUST be listed in the autosync list and the second in the auxiliary list.

In SDP, aptx goes in a=rtpmap with the rate and channel count. variant, bitresolution and the optional channel parameters go in a=fmtp, and ptime goes in a=ptime. In the offer/answer model (RFC 3264) the only negotiable parameter is the delivery method; all others are declarative and MUST NOT be altered in an answer.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a label on the audio saying how fast it was recorded, how many speakers it is for, and which secret settings were used, so the listener can set up the right decoder.

sections.title: Security and Error Resilience
sections.content:
The format inherits the security considerations of RTP and its profiles, so confidentiality comes from encryption. Since the coding is applied end to end, encryption can be done after coding without conflict.

The RFC notes that denial-of-service attacks using hard-to-decode packets are a concern for codecs with uneven decoding load, but apt-X does not show significant non-uniformity. It also states that because both codecs are constant bit rate, the vulnerability that RFC 6562 describes for variable bit rate codecs with secure RTP does not apply.

The codecs have no built-in error control. Generic RTP forward error correction (RFC 5109, RFC 2733) can add resilience to packet loss at the cost of a higher bit rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking the audio in a box works the same as for any other call. The squeezer does not make the listener work extra hard, so bad guys cannot easily jam it up with tricky packets.
